translationRepairs: Thereupon Dou Yan, acting head of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, memorialized that His Majesty's great-great-grandfather, Lord Wen'an of Wen Prefecture, should be titled Emperor Wenxian, temple name Xizu;
Thereupon Dou Yan, acting head of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, memorialized that His Majesty's great-great-grandfather, Lord Wen'an, should be titled Emperor Wenxian, temple name Xizu;
文安府君 is the deceased-official honorific Lord Wen'an; 府君 is not a prefecture, as the following 中丞府君 and 驍衛府君 confirm.
We humbly request posthumous elevation of four generations—great-great-grandfather and above—and the exalted construction of temple chambers."
We humbly request posthumous elevation of the four generations from the great-great-grandfather and the great-grandfather downward, and the exalted construction of temple chambers."
高、曾四代 names the four ancestral generations headed by the great-great-grandfather and great-grandfather; 'and above' reverses the range away from the four generations actually requested.
Tang's Zhongzong and Ruizong both occupied zhao positions, while Gaozu, Wen, and Wu shared zhao and mu as one generation.
Tang's Zhongzong and Ruizong both occupied zhao positions, while Jingzong, Wenzong, and Wuzong shared zhao and mu as one generation.
敬、文、武 are Jingzong, Wenzong, and Wuzong, not Gaozu; the proposed Jing/Wen/Wu remains too clipped beside the expanded Zhongzong and Ruizong in the same sentence.
Hanlin Academician Song Wo objected: "Since the Three Dynasties, brotherly succession has been common, but zhao and mu in different positions—this we have never seen.
Hanlin Academician Song Shi objected: "Since the Three Dynasties, brotherly succession has been common, but zhao and mu in different positions—this we have never seen.
The speaker is 宋湜, romanized Song Shi; Wo does not correspond to 湜.
Hanlin Academician Song Wo stated: "From the Three Dynasties downward, brotherly succession has been common, but zhao and mu in different positions—this we have never seen.
Hanlin Academician Song Shi stated: "From the Three Dynasties downward, brotherly succession has been common, but zhao and mu in different positions—this we have never seen.
The same 宋湜 is Song Shi in the literal field; Wo is a misreading of 湜.

Wen Jiao, on brotherly succession and storing tablets in flanking chambers, argued: 'If each emperor counts as one generation, one could not sacrifice to one's father—falling short even of a commoner's rites.'"

Wen Qiao, on brotherly succession and storing tablets in flanking chambers, argued: 'If each emperor counts as one generation, one could not sacrifice to one's father—falling short even of a commoner's rites.'"
溫嶠 is Wen Qiao (Qiáo); Jiao is the wrong reading of 嶠.
By ancient rule, the spirits of Xi and Shun should be moved.
By ancient rule, the spirits of Xizu and Shunzu should be moved.
僖、順 abbreviate the Song temple names 僖祖 and 順祖 of the two spirits to be moved, not Xi and the sage-king Shun.
According to antiquity, the spirits of Xi and Shun should be moved.
According to antiquity, the spirits of Xizu and Shunzu should be moved.
The literal likewise takes 僖、順 as Xi and Shun; in this temple-count context they are Xizu and Shunzu.
In our dynasty, before Taizu's shrine Taizong was styled Filial Younger Brother, Zhenzong Filial Son, and the late emperor Filial Grandson.
In our dynasty, at Taizu's shrine Taizong was styled Filial Younger Brother, Zhenzong Filial Son, and the late emperor Filial Grandson.
太祖之室 is the Taizu chamber at which the styles are used; locative 'before' can be read as a temporal sequence the Chinese does not state.
Bian and others rebutted: "From Tang to Zhou temple systems differed, yet all maintained seven generations.
Bian and others rebutted: "From the Tang to the Later Zhou, temple systems differed, yet all maintained seven generations.
自唐至周, after an appeal to recent practice, runs Tang through Later Zhou; the next unit's 自周以上 then turns to classical Zhou, so unglossed 'Zhou' here misleads.
Bian and others rebutted: "From Tang to Zhou, temple systems differed, yet all had seven generations.
Bian and others rebutted: "From the Tang to the Later Zhou, temple systems differed, yet all had seven generations.
The literal 自唐至周 is the same Tang-to-Later-Zhou span, not a backward leap to ancient Zhou.

To destroy his temple and store the tablet in a flanking chamber, displacing the grandfather's honor and installing him below descendants, scarcely accords with filial intent toward ancestors or treating the dead as if living.

To destroy his temple and store the tablet in a flanking chamber, displacing the honor of the ancestral fathers and installing him below descendants, scarcely accords with filial intent toward ancestors or treating the dead as if living.
祖考 is the collective honor of ancestral fathers, not a single grandfather.
Acting head Zhou Mengyang of the Court of Ritual argued: "Generations above Xizu are unknown, Xizu as founding ancestor is beyond doubt, and he should be paired with the Life-Giving Emperor."

Acting head Zhou Mengyang of the Court of Ritual and others argued: "Generations above Xizu are unknown, Xizu as founding ancestor is beyond doubt, and he should be paired with the Life-Giving Emperor."
周孟陽等 marks Zhou Mengyang and others as joint speakers; dropping 等 falsely attributes the memorial to him alone.
In 1078, the office for fixing border and temple ritual submitted a plan for eight temples in separate palaces, with the founding ancestor centered and zhao and mu divided left and right.
In 1078, the office for fixing suburban-altar and temple ritual submitted a plan for eight temples in separate palaces, with the founding ancestor centered and zhao and mu divided left and right.
郊廟 is the suburban (jiao) sacrifice together with the ancestral temples, not a geographic border.

In the sixth month of 1083, Empresses Xiaohui, Xiaozhang, Shude, and Zhanghuai were elevated and enshrined; following Empresses Zhangxian Mingsu and Zhangyi, after the rites they proceeded through the ancestral temple, performing only the elevation-enshrinement honoring rite and sacrifice to the seven household spirits, provisionally suspending the mid-winter offering, ordered by consort succession.

In the sixth month of 1083, Empresses Xiaohui, Xiaozhang, Shude, and Zhanghuai were elevated and enshrined; following Empresses Zhangxian Mingsu and Zhangyi, after the rites they proceeded through the ancestral temple, performing only the elevation-enshrinement honoring rite and sacrifice to the seven household spirits, provisionally suspending the first-month-of-winter offering, ordered by consort succession.
孟冬 is the first month of winter; mid-winter would be 仲冬, so the suspended offering is misdated.
When Tang's Wenzong took the throne, Suzong was moved and Emperor Jing counted as one generation—the precedent is not remote.
When Tang's Wenzong took the throne, Suzong was moved and Jingzong counted as one generation—the precedent is not remote.
敬宗 is the temple name Jingzong; 'Emperor Jing' truncates that title and blurs which Tang emperor is meant.

Hence Shang and Zhou, because Qi and Ji had merit in the age of Tang and Yu, called them ancestors of merit; but if merit alone made one an ancestor, then the Xia would not have sacrificed at the border to Gun.

Hence Shang and Zhou, because Qi and Ji had merit in the age of Yao and Shun, called them ancestors of merit; but if merit alone made one an ancestor, then the Xia would not have sacrificed at the border to Gun.
唐 and 虞 are the dynastic designations of Yao and Shun in this ancient chronological pairing, not Tang of Shang and Yu the Great.
Shang and Zhou honored Qi and Ji as ancestors of merit for their service in the age of Tang and Yu; but if merit alone made one an ancestor, the Xia would not have sacrificed at the border to Gun.
Shang and Zhou honored Qi and Ji as ancestors of merit for their service in the age of Yao and Shun; but if merit alone made one an ancestor, the Xia would not have sacrificed at the border to Gun.
The idiomatic field repeats the same mistaken identities: 唐、虞 conventionally denotes the age of Yao and Shun.
